source.title: The Limitations of Large Width in Neural Networks: A Deep Gaussian Process Perspective

page_placements.theme: Bayesian width scaling and prior mismatch

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary information are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps network width and measures test performance, but does not use the original double-descent setup or test whether a peak occurs at the interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The paper reports width sweeps and test RMSE or accuracy for its own models. It also cites double descent as related work, but cited results are not extracted. Kernel-fit measurements and posterior log-likelihood results are not included as rows here because they are not test error or accuracy. The paper does not sweep epochs or test whether increasing sample size raises error near interpolation.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps width in trained deep networks (MNIST MLPs, CIFAR-10 ResNets) and reports test accuracy. Most of each sweep lies in the over-parameterized regime, where V1's second descent should hold. Under fixed, non-negligible L2, accuracy peaks and then degrades with width. With very small L2, wider models do better. The authors argue this limits the 'bigger is better' regime to near-unregularized training. The interpolation threshold is never located, so the peak itself is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that large width can be detrimental: Deep GPs collapse to single-layer GPs, and posteriors lose data-adaptivity as width grows. Bayesian NNs and L2-regularized networks degrade past a 'sweet spot': ≤16 units on small UCI data, about 500–1,000 for CIFAR-10 ResNets. They say this does not hold for models with little or no L2, where the interpolation (double-descent) analysis of Belkin et al. is likely the better model. Wider models may still win through optimization effects.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines width effects in Deep GPs, Bayesian neural networks, and L2-regularized neural networks; it does not reproduce the original double-descent measurements or sweep the interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported width-performance relationship changes with L2 regularization: the paper reports a distinct accuracy maximum for larger regularization, while wider models tend to perform better for smaller regularization. Performance optima also vary by dataset and model family.

fits_no_version.finding: Bayesian NNs and Deep GPs sampled with NUTS on six UCI datasets (N≤1000): test RMSE and log-likelihood are best at small widths (NN 8–16 units, Deep GP 1–2) and degrade toward the limiting GP as width grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Bayesian (non-interpolating) hierarchical models, wider models perform worse once they have sufficient capacity, converging to the limiting GP.

record.problems: The width plots do not report an interpolation threshold or establish the complete double-descent curve. Several relevant curve values are available only in figures. Regression training sets were subsampled to N ≤ 1000. The authors also report that NUTS sampling can perform poorly for width-1 Deep GPs, and that low-regularization or non-Bayesian models may not follow their theoretical account.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's Deep GP width sweeps (Figures 3, 9–11), posterior kernel-fit and log-likelihood results, and the MNIST N=500 panel are not separately extracted: the Deep GP and kernel-fit results do not directly measure neural-network test error, and the N=500 panel's setting is not stated clearly enough to assign separate conditions. No reported epoch-wise or near-interpolation sample-size sweep was found.

untested.parts: Location of a test-error peak at the interpolation threshold, and the initial under-parameterized descent. The threshold is never identified.
No sample-size sweep near interpolation. The N=500/5,000/50,000 MNIST panels are not analysed as a sample-wise effect.
Non-network model classes are not swept past interpolation. Deep GPs are nonparametric with no interpolation threshold.
No label-noise manipulation, no multiple peaks. L2 is fixed, not optimally tuned, so peak removal under optimal regularization is untested.

missing.what: MNIST N=500 panel of the 3-layer MLP width sweep, at the same L2 values. This is a third sample size for the same trend.

record.verdict_notes: The study does not locate the interpolation threshold, so the peak is untested. Its V1 bearing is limited to the regime well past interpolation. The paper explicitly says it does not disagree with double-descent work and attributes that work to the low-regularization setting. The CIFAR ResNet optimum is stated as 500–1,000 in the text but ≤500 in the Fig 4 caption.

versions.untested_parts: The width sweeps measure test RMSE or accuracy, but do not identify the interpolation threshold or establish that a peak is near it; they do not show the full fall-rise-fall curve across and beyond that threshold.

relation.reason: Its own width sweeps measure held-out accuracy in optimized deep networks and bear on V1's large-width behavior.

tranche.reason: The study supplies results and an argument that additional width can harm performance after sufficient capacity, requiring qualification of a general large-width improvement claim.

source_check.notes: No interpolation threshold or complete double-descent curve is identified; the V1 evidence concerns large-width trends at fixed regularization. Figure 4 labels ResNets Adam, but Appendix H explicitly specifies SGD; its caption and main text also differ on the optimal-width bound.

statements.correction: Section 6.1: two-layer Bayesian NNs usually maximize test log likelihood at 8–16 hidden units. Section D.3: three-layer Bayesian NNs maximize log likelihood and kernel fit at ≤8 units per hidden layer. Deep GPs: width 1 or 2 summarized as optimal; width 2 generally best empirically. Section D.2: NUTS struggles with width-1 Deep GPs. Figures 10–11: width generally harms RMSE; exact optima are figure-only. Training N≤1000.
statements.problem: The 8–16-unit optimum is reported for two-layer Bayesian NNs, not all listed Bayesian NNs. Three-layer NNs have a different reported optimum; the width-1 Deep-GP result also has an inference caveat.
